speechtext:
It affords me much pleasure indeed to second the amendment which has just been moved by my hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I. (Mr. Warburton), more especially as it contains exactly the same idea embodied in a resolution that I moved in this House in 1908. As my hon. friend has said, it does equal justice to every province in the Dominion, and calls for no exceptional action in favour of any one province. I may say that I was somewhat surprised to hear some of the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). He went into the matter very vigorously, but I do not think that he studied his subject very thoroughly before he delivered himself on the floor of this House. I expected something a little different from the chivalry and generosity of the west than the evidence that a member from that country was willing to accept favours for his own province and neighbouring provinces which other provinces of this Dominion do not, and have not, enjoyed; but when the lower provinces down by the sea ask to have that treatment continued which was promised to them at the time of confederation, the hon. gentleman threatens if this justice is done to put on his hat and leave the House. I want to remind him that when Alberta and Saskatchewan were admitted to this confederation under the Autonomy Bills, one of the clauses of those Bills provided specifically that fo-r subsidy purposes the population of those two provinces should never be less than a certain figure; although Alberta had not at that time, and I do not suppose she has at this time, the population on which that subsidy was and is reckoned. Therefore I was a little astonished at some of the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, upon whom I have always looked with a good deal of favour as a gentleman of wide views, and not of the narrow views which he propounded to the House this afternoon. I am afraid he has been taking his brief from the Minister of Justice, because I saw the Minister of Justice alongside of him this afternoon, and he has propounded the same ideas that the Minister of Justice propounded in 1907, namely, that the whole scheme of confederation was adopted by the maritime provinces on the one broad principle of representation by population. I wish to say, Mr. Sneaker, that that principle was never recognized nor adopted by the people of New Brunswick. When the Quebec scheme was laid before the people of New Brunswick, they voted _ against it by a large majority. When this question was up on a previous occasion, I read some of the remarks of the then Attorney General, afterwards Sir Albert J. Smith, a member of the Mackenzie administration in this House. On the 20th of March, 1866,

when he was Attorney General in the Legislative Assembly, he said:
He would not vote for any scheme that proposed to base representation on population, unless there is some check in it that will prevent the interests of New Brunswick from being swamped by Canada.
You may smile, Mr. Speaker, at the idea that the people of New Brunswick should be afraid of being swamped by Canada in voting power-for in pre-confederation days the old provinces were known to us as Canada. What was the condition of affairs then? The people of the lower provinces had very few relations with the upper provinces, Quebec and Ontario; there was no intermingling of the people. Our business was carried on across the ocean, and with the people of New England States and New York and other seaboard states. They had very little business with the rest of Canada, and there is no doubt that when this matter was brought up they did fear that their interests would be swamped by an increased population in that of Quebec and Ontario. Then if we take Canada as it is now, why, Sir, the people of those provinces never supposed, any more than did the reverend gentleman whose statements were read this afternoon, that the great country west of Ontario to the Rocky mountains was anything else but an inhospitable region unable to support population, and incapable of settlement. I might remind hon. gentlemen, especially those sitting opposite, that even for a number of years after 1867, there were loud cries that it was utterly silly and foolish to build the Canadian Pacific railway through that country, because it was sterile, it was fit for nothing but to be the home of the wolf and the bear. I have no doubt hon. members will recall some such statements as that. Mr. Smith, then, Attorney General, two days afterward said, in the Legislative Assembly:
I'll go down in the ship rather than consent to representation by population, as contained in the Quebec scheme; but I have no objection to going for it, provided there is a check in the formation of the TJpper House, or otherwise, that will serve to protect the interests of New Brunswick.
In the following month, a large public meeting was held in St. John on the same subject and the Hon. Peter Mitchell, afterwards well known in the history of Canada and I think the first Minister of Marine, said as was reported in the St. John 'Telegram ' of April 21, 1866, as follows:
Hon. Peter Mitchell at last night's public meeting, stated, ' Government would not insist on Quebec scheme of confederation; they would accept such improvements as could be had, and would be willing to allow delegates chosen from both political parties, to go as delegates to the British government to urge

such changes and alterations as might meet the views of the maritime provinces.'
That was done. On June 26 a resolution was introduced in the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick to the following effect:
Resolved, that an humble address be presented to His Excellency the Lieutenant Governor praying that His Excellency will be pleased to appoint delegates to unite with delegates from the other provinces in arranging with the imperial government for the union of British North America

Not on the Quebec scheme,
-but upon such terms as will secure the just rights and interests of New Brunswick, accompanied with provision for the immediate construction of the Intercolonial railway.
The province of Nova Scotia passed a resolution identically the same except that it made no reference to the Intercolonial railway. That will, I think, give the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) an idea that there was a great disinclination and a determination not to accept the principle of representation by population out and out. What was the result? In accordance with this resolution delegates were sent to the old country. They attended the London conference, and this difficulty of the representation of the maritime provinces was the great stumbling block in the negotiations. An effort was made to introduce something into the Act that would serve as a check, as Sir Albert Smith and the Hon. Peter Mitchell urged, on the idea of representation by population, so that the maritime provinces should not lose their representation, if, as was expected, they did not increase in population as rapidly as the other provinces. Hon. George Brown, who has been spoken of as the great advocate of representation by population, and who certainly took a very active part in this confederation scheme, wag troubled over the conditions with which they were met by the fact of these maritime provinces not being willing to consent to that scheme in its entirety, preferring rather to keep out of confederation altogether than to go in with the knowledge that in a few short year3 their voting influence and their representative influence in the parliament of Canada would be so weakened that it would be really swamped. The result was the framing of subsection 4, section 51, and known as the saving clause which is as follows:
On any such readjustment the number of memb?rs for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of any province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.

Mr. Brown thought this clause so valuable that he said of it ' The practical result will be that while lower Canada certainly will not be less, and the lower provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of their representatives.'
Then comes the question, what is ' The number of the aggregate population of Canada ' To find what comprised Canada, you have only to look at the third section of the British North America Act. That sections reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, to declare by proclamation that, on and after a day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this Act, the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall form and be one Dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that day those three provinces shall form and be one Dominion under that name accordingly.
Under that saving clause the maritime provinces joined confederation. What has been the result? They have found that their charter has been broken, that this saving clause which was put in to prevent their losing representatives has been made of no effect whatever by the subsequent amendments which have been made to the British North America Act, including the population of all the rest of Canada, instead of that merely of the four provinces. The result of that has been that whereas if the original Aot of 1867 had been carried out, we would not have lost our representatives, on account of these amendments being read into the Act, and the great population that has been brought into Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and these other parts which have been included in the Dominion of Canada we have been robbed of our representatives when we ought to have been protected by this parliament. It was on account of these amendments being read into the old Act that the Privy Council decided as it did, because it gave its decision on the law as they found it. That is the great grievance which we in the maritime provinces have; to use a common expression we have been gold bricked by these various amendments which, without our knowledge and consent, have been made to the British North America Act. We cannot seek redress in the law courts, we have to appeal to this parliament as the great high court of equity, constituted to redress the grievances of any part of the' Dominion.
Let me refer to the effect which the enlargement of the province of Quebec will have, if it has not already had, on the unit of representation. In 1907, when the Minister of Justice spoke on this question, he declared that there was no doubt in the wotM that the Quebec which was considered in the Act of 1867 was the Quebec whose northern boundary was the height of land separating the Hudson bay waters from the St. Lawrence waters, and that being so it requires no argument to show that the additional area added to Quebec affects the unit of representation and gives us of the maritime provinces a very real grievance. In the British North America Act of 1871 there is provision for enlargement of the boundaries of the various provinces, but the very section giving that power states that it can only be done on arrangements being made with any other province affected thereby. The Minister of Justice, in the course of that address, also stated that if the lower provinces were wrongfully dealt with in 1901, they should have protested, and that having kept silent they had no right to complain now. But, we have no reason to suppose that were a protest made at that time it would be heeded. Let me call attention to the fact that in 1905 the legislature of New Brunswick did protest to'this parliament. When the legislation providing for the autonomy of Alberta and Saskatchewan was before the House the New Brunswick legislature protested against the population of these two provinces being also read into the British North America Act so as to be considered when the representation in this parliament was being readjusted. But, the right hon. gentleman and his government paid no attention to that protest although Mr. Tweedie, now the lieutenant governor of the province, and others who are now close to the Prime Minister, were very strong in supporting it. Mr. Tweedie commenced his remarks by blaming those who were form-erlv interested in provincial affairs and who had moved to the higher political sphere forgetting their province when they came to this Dominion parliament, but I will not refer to that part of his speech. He said:
' At the time of confederation Quebec had certain well defined boundaries. According to the census of 1871, it had an area of 193,555 square miles. Quebec is the province by which the representation of the other provinces is regulated. In 1898 an Act was passed which extended the boundaries of Quebec so that it contained 351,000 square miles, an addition of
158,000	square miles to its territory. This territory thus added to Quebec is that territory through which the Grand Trunk Pacific will pass, and which we may expect to beoome populous in the future. The result will be to diminish our representation in a way never contemplated by the British North America Act.'
I call the attention of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) to that statement. On the same occasion in the New Brunswick legislature there was a speech also made by a gentleman, who, however we may differ about him in other respects,

we all agree is a very able lawyer, and anything he states in his legal capacity commands attention. I refer to the Hon. Wm. Pugsley who is now Minister of Public Works, and who was then Attorney General of the province, and who speaking to the resolution moved in the legislature of Jfew Brunswick in 1905, said:
I have never entertained the slightest doubt that the fathers of confederation in framing their scheme of representation intended that it should be confined to the four original provinces of Canada, and that if other provinces were admitted it should be on terms. In that view I was fortified by the statement of one of the greatest statesmen of Canada, who was himself one of the fathers of confederation, and who took a leading part in bringing it about. I refer to the late Sir John A. Macdonald who in his report of the 29th December, 1870, on the admission of the Northwest Territory said:
' The general purview of the British North America Act of 1867 seems to be confined to the four provinces upper and lower Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick originally forming the Dominion/
I call these words specially to the notice of the right hon. the Prime Minister because I understand that he once held- whether he does now or not I do not know -a different view, and that he contended that Canada was not originally confined to the four provinces but included all that might be added at any time since. Then the Hon. Mr. Pugsley also said:
When British Columbia was admitted into the union it was stipulated that her representation should be increased under the terms of the British North America Act and that this Act should apply as if she had been one of the original provinces of the confederation, the same thing was done with respect to Manitoba. Now what has been the effect of this? It is that you must construe the British North America Act as if these provinces had been in the union in 1876.'
' If that is so, the compact of confederation has been violated by legislation and by order in council without being consulted. Surely the authorities at Ottawa should see that this wrong is remedied.
If the population of the territories and of British Columbia had been excluded New Brunswick would not have lost a representative.'	'
' Some may say it will be difficult to have the wrong done us righted, but I think that it can be. I have faith in the sense of justice of those administering the affairs of the Dominion.'
' I can only repeat what I said yesterday, that the province of New Brunswick entered into confederation with Quebec with certain defined boundaries, and that it was never contemplated that a Quebec should be created double the size of the original province. Yet Quebec is the pivotal province upon which the representation of this province depends. I feel that they have done us a great wrong, yet I do not despair but that when the mat-Mr. DANIEL.
ter is brought to the notice of the government and the parliament, some steps will bo taken to see that this injustice is not continued.'
I believe that Saint Paul says that faith is the substance of things hoped for, and I hope that my hon. friend, the hon. Minister of Public Works, who has that faith, will also obtain the substance of the things which we hope for, and will be able, through his influence in the Cabinet, to have righted some of the wrongs to which we have been referring this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, when you left the Chair at six o'clock I had just read the opinions and statements uttered in the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick with regard to the matter under discussion by the then Attorney General of New Brunswick, and now the Minister of Public Works in this government. When a gentleman of his well known legal ability expresses an opinion, it must be received with the greatest respect.
The subject we have before us to-night is an amendment asking that the minimum representation of every province in the Dominion, or which hereafter may join the Dominion, shall never be less than the representation given to it at the time ' of its admission. In other words, that would apply the principle to all the provinces which now applies to British Columbia. The principle of course is not a new one. It is carried out in the constitution of the Australian commonwealth, and I believe it is given effect to in the United States not alone with regard to the Senate but also with regard to congress. The idea is also embodied, as I stated before six o'clock, in our law regarding subsidies for the new provinces, in which it was provided that no matter how much smaller the population of the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan should become, their subsidies would never be less than those provided in the Acts creating these provinces.
I have spoken about the protest which was sent to His Excellency the Governor General and thfe Privy Council and also to the right hon. the Prime Minister against the admission of the population of the new provinces into the British North America Act, so that it might also be counted against the lower provinces when their representation came to be adjusted. I shall not read the preamble but will place the protest on ' Hansard.'	The
preamble	recites the fact that	the

Privy Council left undecided the question whether the population of the territories should be included in the nopulation of Canada, under subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act. It refers to the fact that the imperial order in council admitting British Columbia and the statute admitting Manitoba provided that the British North America Act of 1867 should apply to them as if they formed part of the original confederation, thus prejudicing the position of the original parties to the agreement. It refers to the enlargement of the boundaries of the province of Quebec without making provision for the effect thereof on the other provinces, and the resolution which was passed unanimously by the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick is as follows:
Resolved, that in the opinion of this House the earnest attention of the government of Canada should be drawn to the effect of the said order in council and statutes, respectively, relating to the admission to the union of British Columbia and Manitoba, and it should be requested to take such action as may be necessary in order to restore the four original provinces to the position in which they would have been but for the order in council and legislation passed subsequently to the Act of 1867 in respect to which, such provinces were not consulted, and to which they were not parties. (2) That in the Act for the creation of the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan it should not be provided that the Act should apply to them as if they were in the union originally, and the rights of the original provinces as to revision should not be affected by the creation of such new provinces. (3) That the injustice to the other provinces, particularly New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, which have no opportunity for enlargement of their areas, it should have been provided, and should now be provided, that for purposes of representation the boundaries of Quebec, the population o" which is the basis of representation, should be deemed to be as they were at the time of confederation, or that some just and equitable provision should be made to save the other original provinces and also Prince Edward Island from loss in the .representation. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Prime Minister.
I noticed, when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) was speaking this afternoon, that he threw out his chest and with an air of great importance informed the House and the country that he represented 45,000 people. Well, let me tell the hon. gentleman that quite a number of members in this House represent 45,000 people and more. I represent that number myself and I never thought it necessary to proclaim the fact as did the hon. gentleman. My hon. friend from Cumberland
(Mr., Rhodes) represents a constituency which has at least 50,000 people. No doubt the constituency of Westmorland, New Brunswick contains over 45,000 inhabitants. There is the constituency of Cape Breton South which has as large a population. I think, as Cumberland, while Halifax county of Nova Scotia, is the largest con-tituency in the whole Dominion. So that there was no reason for my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) being so chesty, more especially when we take into account the class of people he represents. The people we represent in the maritime provinces are the descendants of the early settlers-English, Scotch, Irish and French. But who does my hon. friend represent? He represents, to a large extent, Galicians, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Buckowinians, and possibly Doukhobors, all new comers, a great many exceedingly illiterate, not able to speak the language of the country and unacquainted with its constitution. But because he represents some 45,000 of these people, largely the flotsam and jetsam of southern Europe, my hon. friend has all the assertiveness of a grand pasha, and strives to place himself on a par or above par as compared with the representatives of constituencies such as we have in the martitime provinces. Sir, I think there is no comparison between them whatever. But even if we consider only number and not quality, my hon. friend is not a representative of more people than the average member from the maritime provinces.
What we are asking for is what we believe to be the simplest ways of remedying the injustice to which we have hitherto been obliged to submit. There can be no doubt that it is an injustice. Where there is a legal wrong there should be a legal remedy, and that legal remedy cannot be found in our courts, it cannot be found in the Privy Council, the only place where it can be found is this parliament.
And we make this appeal, not for charity, not for something to which we are not entitled; we make our appeal for the granting of our legal rights, rights which have been taken away from us 'by legislation passed by the imperial parliament at the instance of this parliament; we ask for equity and right treatment from this parliament as the only means by which that .wrong can he righted. I do not wish to take up more of the time of the House. I have, on one ot two occasions, spoken on this subject. It is one that I think very much of, and it is of most signal importance to the people of the maritime provinces. It has not, perhaps, reached the stage of agitation to any great extent yet, but I am quite satisfied that, unless justice is dope to us in this resnect, agitation will arise in the maritime provinces and that it will continue to aggrandize and enlarge itself until the peo-

pie of the maritime provinces, in so far as the rest of the Dominion is concerned, will show themselves to he in a very dissatisfied condition. And I think it would he far better for this parliament to use good judgment now, at a time when it can be done without any straining, without any complaint, with good-will to all. I have a great deal of confidence, as I stated, in the opinion expressed by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). We have in the present cabinet, as has already been mentioned, three members from the maritime provinces, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden), every one of them the holder of a very important portfolio. I cannot but believe that if these hon. gentlemen use the influence that they have with the other hon. members of the government of Canada, there can be no doubt that the justice which we are asking for, the equity which we appeal for, will be done, and that at no distant day.

I have not figured that up. We are going to make no changes; if I thought we were, I would perhaps spend some time on the mathematics of the question. As a matter of fact, the fathers of confederation did make provision for the falling off in the population of some of the provinces, they could not foresee at that time which provinces they might be, by providing that if the decrease was not greater than five per cent there should be no loss of representation; that was one point. On the other hand, in the composition of the Senate, the maritime provinces were given 24 members, the province of Quebec was given 24, and the province of Ontario was given 24-no question of representation by population entering into the composition of the Senate. The Senate was to be the guardian of provincial rights, and whatever guardianship the Senate is
able to offer at the present time, exists now on that basis, and the maritime provinces are as strong there as ever they were.
One would almost assume, from the discussion in this House to-day, that there was a struggle between the east and the west, and that the east were afraid of los.ing something because we in the west hope, in a few years, largely to increase our population. Mr. Speaker, if there has been any strife between the east and the west it has not entered this House. As a western representative, I think I may say that the proposals of the west, and they have been many, and we have made great demands, we have a great future-these demands have been met in a liberal spirit, by the people of the east. I have always said that on my own platform, and I am going to say it here. The people of the west have never shown any antagonism to the people of the east.	,
Nobody says that they did.
I am inferring that from the argument.
The hon. member has no right to infer anything.

At any rate, I am .denying that such is the case. As long as provincialism is kept out, the east and west will get along together; it is only by the introduction of provincialism that there will be any strife. My hon. friend from St. John spoke about the makeup of the constituency which was represented by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff):	Galicians, Buckowinians,
Doukhobors, Ruthenians-all speaking unknown tongues-if I understood him aright, the flotsam and the jetsam of southern Europe. My hon. friend informs me that he has none of that population in his riding.	.
Four Galicians.

Four Galicians, some Germans, and I have no doubt they can all speak the English language. The argument of my hon. friend is that because the people of the maritime provinces have a better educated ancestry, and are better educated themselves to-day, therefore they should count more in the numerical representation of this parliament than do these communities in the west which are largely made up of foreign population. Well, while these conditions do not exist in the. constituency of my hon. friend from Assiniboia, I may tell you that they do exist in the constituency I have the honour to represent:	French Canadians, Galicians,
Buckowinians, Mennonites, Slovacs, Norwegians, Doukhobors, Americans, Canadians. I am very proud to represent such a constituency growing up in the Northwest

of Canada, and growing, I am proud to say, into a Canadian citizenship which will make them the equal of any population which Canada produces.
My hon. friend from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton) stated that the balance of power in the west was held by people from the maritime provinces. I ain not able to verify that statement, but I hope it is true. Some years ago there was a large emigration from the maritime provinces, and I am sorry to say it was not to the Canadian west, it was largely to the American states. The tide has turned, we are getting a large population from the maritime provinces. I have been struck with the way in which our own Canadian people are coming back from the United States into western Canada. I have run across so many from northern Dakota and northern Minnesota, who, themselves or their parents, emigrated from Ontario, particularly to the western States, and whose children or themselves are returning to Canada, that, in my part of the country, when a man tells me that he came from north Dakota or from north Minnesota, I always ask him: What part of Ontario did you come from?
There are some counties in the northern part of north Dakota which I could name where the population is very largely Canadian. My only regret is that we are getting, in many cases, only the children, and that of that good Canadian population which should have come into our west we are getting only a few. I am sorry that we are not repatriating people from the maritime provinces. The maritime province men invariably went into the eastern United States, and they dil not find farm life there congenial to them. Had they gone into the American west, we might have got them, but I am afraid that most of the people from the maritime provinces who went to the United States prior, say, to 1900, are lost to Canada. But times have changed and we are getting them now. I hope it is true, as my hon. friend has said, that the maritime provinces have the balance of power in the west. I think it has always been true that the maritime provinces have held the balance of power in Canada. It has not been because of provincialism on the part of the maritime provinces that they have held that position, it is because their leading men were not provincialists but great Canadians, and I need only point to such names as the Tuppers, father and son; Sir John Thompson and Sir Leonard Tilley. 1 would note that the first lieutenant of the Prime Minister is a Nova Scotia man, the leader of the opposition (Mr. E. L. Borden) is a Nova Scotia man, and his first lieutenant, although representing an Ontario con-

stituency, claims the province of New Brunswick as his birthplace. The Canadi-anism of the maritime provinces has shown itself not only in these great men who have taken part in the political life of this country, but it has shown itself in the way in which they have taken their position in .the interior provinces, in our universities. I need only noint to the fact that the late Sir William Dawson, a Pictou man, was nresident of McGill. The late Principal Grant was a Nova Scotia man, When the Universitv of Toronto wanted a president, they took President Falconer from Nova Scotia. The successor to the late Principal Grant is Dr. Gordon, also a Nova Scotia man. All these go to confirm the statement which my hon. friend makes as applied to Canada as a whole, that the balance of power, in fact I might say the predominating influence in Canada, is a maritime province influence, and I must say, as a Canadian, I am very proud indeed of the maritime province men who have made such a stand.
There is another thing; if the population of the maritime provinces was being lost to Canada, it would be a matter of very great regret not only to the people of the lower provinces, but to us all as good Canadians. We are glad indeed that in our Canadian west we are having maritime province' men in our professions, in our lines of business and in our schools. The Chief Justice of my own province of Saskatchewan, Chief Justice Wetmore, is a New Brunswicker; the Attorney General, Hon. Mr. Turgeon, is a New Brunswicker; the president of the new University of Saskatchewan, opened last September, is Dr. Walter Murray, lately of Dalhousie College.
A New Brunswicker.

And as my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works says, a New Brunswicker. The time will come when the preponderance of population will be west of the Great Lakes, and when the great representation in this House will come from there also.
My hon. friend from Charlottetown (Mr. Warburton) said that he did not think that these maritime province men in the west would see any injustice done to the maritime provinces. I am sure they will not. As western men, they are not provincialists, you will not find them standing out for Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta against the east. I think you will find them big Canadians, willing to do their share in the progress of the maritime provinces, as well as in that of the Canadian west in which they are living. The only danger in which we are in the west is from provincialism. I do not think that such a resolution as is put forward by my hon. friend, with its amendment, is going to

put down provincialism. It is said by these bon. gentlemen that if we only make the changes which they suggest we shall have peace, that can be the only object of the discussion which they have brought on. I believe that if their proposals were acceded to, we would have the same kind of peace after 25 years that they had when the Canadas were united and when the basis of representation was fixed in the Act of British North America by the men who then struggled for some new form of government to get out of a dilemma. I have only to say, in conclusion, that so long as there is no provincialism, and so long as there is a Canadian spirit, east and west will work together. It matters little as to the numbers of the representatives that are in this House, it matters very much as to the kind of representatives who are here. I have no doubt that in the future the maritime provinces will do as they have done in the past, and send us their very best, and if they do that, if they send the kind of representative that has always been here, there will be no danger at all to the interests of the maritime provinces.
I may say that if this question comes to a vote I shall be bound to vote against both the motion and the amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. O. S. CROCKET (York, New Brunswick).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to add my voice to what has already been said on behalf of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I., (Mr. War-burton), and seconded by my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel). It seems to me that the mover and seconder of this amendment have made out a case which must appeal to that sense of justice and fair play which, aside from party questions, ought to animate this parliament in its deliberations. The mover and seconder of this resolution have shown that the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were in a peculiar situation when the confederation compact was negotiated, they were small provinces, with small areas, with no opportunity of expansion of any kind. They could not possibly hope to keep abreast with the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec in the increase of their population. These two small provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were giving up the control of their own affairs with respect to which they formerly had full and plenary powers; they were assigning to the large Dominion parliament in which they were to be greatly outnumbered the control of their trade and commerce, their criminal laws, the right of taxation, and the other important subjects which are assigned to this parliament by the terms of the Confederation Act. In return for that they asked some slight concessions, and 38
I think it will be agreed by any student of the history of the confederation conferences, that these concessions were practically agreed to by the delegates from Ontario and Quebec. The concession which they chiefly asked was a slight modification of the principle of representation by population. There can be no doubt-I do not deny it, and I do not think it will be denied by anybody-that representation [DOT]by population was laid down as the guiding principle of representation when this confederation was formed. But the delegates from the smaller provinces insisted that there should be some modification of that principle, and the modification which was assented to by the delegates representing the four original provinces is to be found in section 51 of the British North America Act which I propose to put oil record, because, although subsection 4 has been referred to, there is a point in the first subsection which is important in this discussion:
On the completion of the census in. the year 1871, and on each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces-
I would wish the House to mark this:
-the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such a manner and from such time, as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides subject and according to the following rules:- (1) Quebec shall have the fixed number of 65 members.
(2)	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number of 65 bears to the num-b<?r of population of Quebec. (so ascertained)
(3)	In the computation of the number of
members for a proyince as a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded:	but a fractional
part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole nnmber.
And this is the subsection which has been spoken of as the saving clause and offered to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia as a guarantee against diminution of representation:
On any such readjustment the number
of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of tlie aggregate imputation of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province as ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
That is the section that covers the representation of the different provinces in this House. It will be seen that the original British North America Act contemplated only four provinces and that this

[DOT]very section uses the expression ' four provinces.' The agreement and the compact was so entered into between these four provinces. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel) and my hon. friend from Charlottetown (Mr. Warburton) quoted the declarations which were made by Mr. Galt and the Hon. George Brown upon this question, and the declarations which were made in the legislatures of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island with reference to the contention which those provinces were making. They felt there was a danger in giving up the control of their affairs to such a large parliament as this that they would be outnumbered, and that they could not keep abreast with the increase of the population of Ontario and Quebec. It will not, I think, be disputed by any member of this House that that was the position which those delegates took. When the principle of representation by population was under discussion they made'this claim and subsection 4 of section 51 was offered to the delegates of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as a sure and certain safeguard against any reduction of the representation of these provinces. And Mr. Speaker, it would have been a sure and certain safeguard had it not been for the developments which have taken place since and which could not possibly have been foreseen at that time. They were far-seeing statesmen in those days, but how could they possibly have divined the wonderful development and growth of the Northwest Territories? Since that compact was entered into no less than five provinces have been admitted to the union with the result that that which was offered to the delegates of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as an absolute safeguard against any redaction of their representation has been practically read out of the Act. Another thing which occurred after the confederation conferences which had its effect in altering the conditions, was the extension of the boundaries of the province of Quebec. Quebec was made the pivotal province so far as representation was concerned and the province of Quebec had the advantage of having a minimum representation fixed.
And a maximum as well.

And a maximum as well. But so far as Ontario and New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were concerned they accepted subsection 4 of section 51 as a protection in that particular. It was felt in the maritime provinces, as I think all members of the House will agree, that in order to have effective representation in the large federal parliament composed of upwards of 190 members there must be a minimum of representation fixed. It was felt in New Brunswick Mr CROCKET
that to ensure effective representation of that province and the exercise of the fair influence to which that province was entitled in the confederacy, we should have at least fifteen members, and, the people of Nova Scotia in like manner felt they should have at least nineteen members. That was the representation which was assigned to these provinces at the union, with this saving clause, that there should be no reduction unless the proportion which the population of each of those provinces should bear to the aggregate population of Canada should be reduced by a one-twentieth part or over. Take the case of the last census; it is true that had the population of Canada been reckoned under the terms of that section as it was embodied in the original Confederation Act and made applicable only to the four original provinces: Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, neither Nova Scotia nor New Brunswick would have lost a member as actually happened.
It was only for the reason I have pointed out, that five new provinces have since been admitted to this union, that this result took place. I appeal to the hon. members of this House, if it strikes them as fair or equitable that that expression 'four provinces' in that section of the British North America Act should be construed to mean nine provinces. That is, however, just what the judgment of the Judicial Committee, of the Privy Council means. Although the expression 'four provinces' was used in that section on which we rely, the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada held that in consequence, not of anything contained in the original Act to which we were parties, but of amendments having been made in it afterwards, with reference to which we had not been consulted, the meaning of the section was changed. I ask hon. members if it is fair or equitable that, although that was held, in the very judgment that has been referred to, to be the meaning at the time, we should be held bound by a change of that meaning effected by legislation to which we were not parties at all. My hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) has stated, in his very able argument this afternoon, that the judgment of the court proceeded upon that ground; and in order that hon. members may see that his contentions were well founded, I am going to read a few brief extracts from the judgment of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. Perhaps I should first point out that the amendments to which I refer as having been subsequently made to this Act were the amendments made to the Imperial Act of 1871, the Act of 1875 and the Act of 1886. Mr. Justice Davies, in the course of his judgment, used this language:

After careful consideration of the whole Act, and its amendments, I have concluded that the expression ' four provinces ' means and must he construed as ' several provinces.'
I Rave no doubt, reading into this Act those subsequent amendments, that that is a sound judgment, and that technically and legally Mr. Justice Davies was quite right; but I ask this House to consider this question, not upon strict legal grounds -because we all recognize that in strict law we are bound by this judgment-but whether that is a construction by which in equity we should be bound, when the courts of this country hold that the expression 'Canada', consisting of four provinces means for the purpose of the readjustment of our representation ' Canada consisting of nine provinces.' Further, he said:
If any reasonable doubts did exist as to the true meaning of the sections under review, this subsequent imperial legislation would seem to remove them.
That the judgment of Mr. Justice Davies was based, not on the original Confederation Act, but on the subsequent amendments which were made without the smaller provinces consenting thereto is abundantly clear from these extracts. Further on, Mr. Justice Davies said:
Upon the whole, after careful consideration, I am of the opinion that after the admission of new provinces and territories into the union, the expression 'Canada' and ' provinces ' throughout the Act of 1867 must, unless specially restricted by the context, be necessarily given an interpretation different from that which they respectively bore before these provinces and territories were admitted.
Then there was the judgment of the chief justice, Sir Elzear Taschereau:
It may be well that the framers of the British North America Act have not foreseen or provided for every possible eventuality in the positions of the different provinces of the Dominion as to population or other matters; it may be that some provinces would have refused to join the union had they foreseen all the results that their adhesion to it is now ascertained to carry, but with such considerations we are not here con cerned.
A very proper dictum in a judgment determining a matter on strict legal principles; but I ask hon. members of this House whether such considerations are those by which the parliament of Canada should be bound.
Now, I must express my very great surprise at the opposition to this resolution which has come from hon. members from western Canada. I was particularly surprised at the speech of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), who frankly stated that he did not know very much about the legal aspect of the case, and I 881
think that before he concluded he convinced the House that that statement was absolutely correct. What astonished me more than anything else was the threat which that hon. gentleman made that he would resign his seat in this House if this proposal were adopted. The hon. gentleman based his whole argument upon an assumption which I have shown was erroneous. He dealt with this matter as if the maritime provinces were appealing to this House as a matter of favour or grace. That is not the situation at all. It might possibly appear to be so from the terms of the original resolution, and I quite concur in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that to be logical and consistent, we should ask for the restoration of the representation which was assigned to us when we entered the union. I think, from what has been stated so well by my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) and my hon. friend from the city of Charlottetown (Mr. Warburton), and from the quotations which I have read from the judgments of the Supreme Court, the hon. member for Assiniboia should recognize that we are not asking this matter as a favour. We are asking that a positive injustice which has been done to the maritime provinces in the matter of its representation be remedied by this parliament, and it is only upon that ground that such a request could be made. We think that has been fully established, and I have listened in vain for anything either in the speech of my hon. friend from Assiniboia or the speech of my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), which in any way meets the case which has been so well made out by the mover and the seconder of this resolution. Those hon. gentlemen spoke as if we were seeking to disturb the principle of representation by population and to alter the terms of the British North America Act. We are not seeking to do anything of the kind. We are asking to have restored to us a right of which we have been deprived by the amendments to the British North America Act to which I have referred, and by the admission of five new provinces into this confederation, which, under the meaning of that Act as it was passed and as it was accepted by the delegates from the maritime provinces, was never intended to enter into the calculation when the question of the readjustment of the representation in this parliament should be dealt with. I deprecate the position which my hon. friend from Assiniboia took. I do not think he breathes the snirit or gives voice to the sentiment of the west on this question. I know certainly of one hon. member from the west who, after hearing the very able speech of my hon. friend from St. John
27G7

(Mr. Daniel) this afternoon said that the latter had made out a good case and that so far as he was concerned he would, as a representative of the west, vote for it. I would put the question to my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) whether members from the east are disposed to deal with a question affecting the west in the same spirit as the hon. gentleman displayed this afternoon. If they did, what would become of this parliament? Can the hon. gentleman point to any occasion in which the east has shown any disposition whatever to treat the west with anything else than the utmost generosity?
Has the west ever shown any disposition to treat the east with anything hut fair play, justice and generosity.

It is not very often that representatives from the east demand anything from this parliament. This is one of the first things we have asked since I have been a member, and the first voice raised against that request is that of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and he is not content with simply opposing it, but threatens to resign his seat if it be granted. I do not know that I could retaliate by threatening to resign mine if it be not granted. I do not think that would have very much effect, but it would certainly create a very interesting situation if some of our good Liberal friends from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island would threaten to resign if this measure of justice should be denied them. I have confidence in the fairness and the justice of this House upon questions that are not party questions, and I am convinced that members of this House who have studied this question and have followed the debate, must be themselves convinced that a case has been made out to which no adequate answer has been or can be made.

I wish t-o say a few words in support of the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton). The question now under consideration has been brought up in this House on several occasions. I understand that in the session of 1907, and also in 1908, a lengthy discussion took place with regard to this question of representation. In the province from which I have the honour to come, it is one that has been agitating the minds of the people for a considerable time. You are all aware that Prince Edward Island was very reluctant to join confederation, and it was only after some years of discussion and considerable agitation that it decided to throw in its lot with the union. But there was one question standing out very prominently that is, the question of representation and we were not anxious to enter confederation Mr. CROCKET.
unless we were assured that we would have six representatives in this House for all time to come. I do not think it necessary*, to read the despatches and telegrams which were passed at the time the negotiations were going on for the purpose of bringing Prince Edward Island into the union, as these have been already presented to the House and to the country. But there can be no doubt that the intention was to give Prince Edward Island six members for all time to come, and when, on the readjustment in 1891, we lost one member, there was very much dissatisfaction in our province. There was, however, a strong belief in the minds of the people that some measure would be taken to rectify what was considered an oversight on the part of our delegates in negotiating the terms of confederation. The matter went before the courts and ultimately to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The decision was adverse to our contention, and now we can only look to the parliament of Canada for redress of what we consider was an error at the time and which is to-day a grievance. Should -we continue to lose our representation in the same ratio as we have done in the past, it will not be many years before we shall have but one or perhaps no representative at all. I do not know what shall be done when that condition cornels about; but if there be a desire to remedy this grievance, this is the opportune time to do it. Our Dominion census will be taken again in June, and after that time there will be no doubt redistribution of. the representation in this House. The present would be, therefore, the best time for this parliament to take some definite steps and have the matter settled. It is not my intention to go over the ground which has been so well covered by the different speakers this afternoon. I rise only to place on record my views on behalf of my constituents in Prince county, Prince Edward Island. Time and again they have urged me to bring this matter before parliament; arid in doing so I am simply discharging a duty which I owe those I represent, and I can only express the strong hope and conviction that this parliament will take such measures as will restore to the maritime provinces the representation they had when they entered confederation. In doing this, parliament would be accomplishing a graceful and generous act. It would re^ move a grievance and do an act of justice which would be very much appreciated and go a long w*ay to remove the discontent now existing in the maritime provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
I think that perhaps it would not be out of place for me to make a few remarks on this very important question, more especially as my hon. friend who seconded the amendment (Mr. Daniel) has referred to the argument I made on the

subject while a member of the provincial legislature and also to the fact that I acted for the province of New Brunswick when the case was argued before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. In my opinion the way in which this matter should be presented is rather along the line taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Richards) than along that taken by my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket). My hon. friend from York said that a great injustice was done the maritime provinces, and he claims that these provinces were not here asking for a favour but demanding, as a matter of right, that a change should be made in the representation.
If my hon. friend will pardon me, I said we were demanding the restoration of a right of which we had been deprived.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say, and I think I understood him correctly, that it is not as a matter of favour, but rather as a matter of right that the representation should be restored to what it was. But it seems to me that my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Richards) has put the matter on the only ground on which it can be put, and that is that it would be a generous thing for the larger provinces to recognize the dissatisfaction existing in the maritime provinces and which is bound to increase as our representation declines. It would be an act of broad generosity, for the larger provinces to recognize that fact, to deal in this spirit with the smaller provinces and to restore the representation to what it was at the time of confederation and below which the people then thought it never would fall. The reason that I say that it cannot be said that an injustice has been done to the lower provinces is that we have no right to complain of what is the interpretation given to the constitution by the highest court of the realm. Under confederation we have a supreme court for the whole Dominion constituted by virtue of the provisions of the constitutional Act, under which the constitution may be interpreted. The question of representation came before that court and that judgment was given. Appeal was taken to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and the Act was interpreted by that tribunal. We are bound by that interpretation; the smaller provinces are as much bound by it as the larger provinces; and no province has any right to complain when the constitution is being lived up to by the provinces of Canada. Therefore, it is that I say we cannot base our claim upon the ground that any injustice has been done to us. When I was arguing the matter in the provincial legislature, upon the occasion to which my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) refers, I was arguing in the light of the constitution as I interpreted it. But I was contending that, according to the true meaning of section 51 of the British North America Act, the ' four provinces ' meant the four provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I thought that was a fair and reasonable interpretation to give to those words. But the Supreme Court of Canada and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council have held otherwise, and we cannot complain of the decision which these courts have given. It is the decision of the highest court in the empire and we are bound to regard that as a correct interpretation.
Was not the argument referred to made after the delivery of the judgment?

One argument was made after the delivery of the judgment, I think, at the time the resolution was passed. But, if I remember rightly, I made an argument before the case went to the Judicial Committee. Possibly an argument was made after, at the time of the resolution which wa,3 forwarded to this parliament and to His Excellency the Governor General.
In 1905 that was.

My hon. friend may have been referring to the latter argument. But I do not know that that alters the case. We cannot complain that any injustice has been done to us by reason of the interpretation that the highest court of the empire has given to the British North America Act. My hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) said that the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has given a decision which has taken away the rights of the maritime provinces, and that that decision was based on legislation put through this parliament by the present government. Now, I was sorry that my hon. friend put the matter upon that ground because I could not help thinking that he was seeking in some way to create prejudice against the present administration by reason of legislation which this government had asked parliament to adopt. If the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rests upon legislation passed subsequent to the British North America Act, that legislation began in the year 1870, some twenty-3ix years before this government came into power

I was quite aware of the time, and mentioned when these Acts were passed. I do not see how the hon. gentleman could understand me as having referred only to what took place after 1896. The thing was monstrous

I am glad to hear my hon. friend's explanation. He said, not only once but twice, that the decision of

the Privy Council had been based upon legislation introduced into this parliament by this government.
This parliament.

The hon. gentleman used the word 'government' perhaps not meaning to do so. I am glad we understand each other. The first legislation was passed in 1870, when it was provided that a portion of Prince Rupert's land, should be carved out and created into the province of Manitoba. And, by section 2 of that Act, these words were used, and upon them the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has laid some stress, as also has the Supreme Court of Canada.
On, from and after the said day on which the order of the Queen in Council should take effect as aforesaid, the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, shall, except those parts thereof which are in terms made, or, by reasonable intendment, may be held to be specially applicable to, or only to affect one or more, but not the whole of the provinces now composing the Dominion, and except so far as the same may be varied by this Act, be applicable to the province of Manitoba, in the same way, and to the_ like extent as they apply to the several provinces of Canada, and as if the province of Manitoba had been one of the provinces originally united by the said Act.
The same language is used in the order in council admitting British Columbia into the union, and the same language was used subsequently when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved out of the Northwest Territories. Therefore, I think no particular responsibility can rest upon one party more than another so far as this parliament is concerned in reference to the legislation enacted here or by the imperial parliament. But, I think that, in considering as to whether or not the judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are such as can properly be complained of we must bear in mind that they rest their judgments to a very large extent upon section 146 of the British North America Act which provides that Prince Rupert's land, British Columbia and also Newfoundland may be taken into the union and become provinces of the Dominion of Canada, and have held that it must be considered that, when the four provinces went into the union they went in with the full knowledge of the fact that Prince Rupert's land, British Columbia and Newfoundland as well might subsequently come into the union, also, that when they did come in, they must come in as if they had originally been provinces of the Dominion, and also that when they did come in the word ' four ' should be held to be eliminated and the number be read as five, six, seven, eight or nine as the case might be, and that regard must be had to all the provinces of Mr. PUGSLEY.
Canada at the time when section 51 and subsection 4 of that section were being interpreted. I do not intend to say very much more, but I would like to express my own opinion that, strongly as I feel upon this subject, strongly as I feel that it is desirable, not alone in the interests of the maritime provinces but in the interests of Canada at large, that the representation of these smaller provinces should not decline, and that in some way, if at all possible, it would be to the interest of Canada that the number should be restored to what it was at the time of confederation, yet I think it would be a most regrettable thing if this resolution were to pass. Suppose, as we can conceive it possible, this were to pass against the wish of the majority of any one of the provinces, it would be regarded as an attempt on the part of the representatives in this parliament to alter the terms of the constitution against the views of the majority of one of the partners to the compact of confederation. That would be a most deplorable result, and it seems to me that, if we are ever going to attain the wishes we have with regard to the representation of the smaller provinces, we must go about it in a different way.
This thought occurs to me, that possibly the proper way to go about it would be to do the same as was done when it was sought to secure an increase in the allowances which were made from the Dominion treasury to the different provinces of Canada. At that time all the provinces were consulted, at that time an interprovincial conference was held, at which representatives of all the provinces of Canada were present. After considerable discussion and deliberation, they agreed among themselves that it was desirable that the British North America Act should be altered as respects the subsidies to the provinces. They passed a resolution, which was submitted to this government, and as a result, a petition was sent to the Imperial parliament praying that the British North America Act should be amended, and that the basis of subsidies to the provinces should be altered. It is possible that some such course might be adopted with regard to representation. It is possible that if the governments of the smaller provinces were to make representations to the provincial governments of the larger provinces, they might be induced to hold a conference of the representatives of the different provinces of Canada, which might agree among themselves with regard to representation; they might pass a resolution and forward it to this government, with the request that it should be laid before parliament to be dealt with. I can well understand that if all the provinces of Canada were unanimous on this question, if they were all to agree

that the representation of the smaller provinces should be restored to what it was at the time of confederation, this government might feel it to be its duty to bring the matter before parliament, and parliament might feel it t-o be its duty to give effect to the unanimous resolution of the representatives of the governments of the various provinces. When the subsidies were readjusted, I remember distinctly it was stated in parliament that this was an agreement which had been come to by the family of provinces, that it was a matter for the provinces to deal with, they had spoken with united voice, and their voice ought to be heeded by this parliament. It may be that if the governments of the different provinces were to speak again with united voices in regard to representation, and if they should unanimously agree that the representation of the smaller provinces should be restored to what it was at the time of confederation, then this parliament could act upon such a resolution. But it seems to me that until that course is taken, it certainly would not be desirable, it would not be proper, and it would be entirely against the best interests of Canada, that the present resolution should be adopted by this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIB (Cape Breton North).
speechtext:
At the commencement of this debate I had no idea that any such an element as sectionalism would enter into it. I am sure that there is no foundation for introducing sectionalism into this discussion; and if the hon. mover of the resolution, or the hon. mover of the amendment, has introduced any argument which might be understood as diminishing any of the powers or possibilities of the west, I am sure it was inadvertently and unintentionally, I do not remember that any such argument was used. But there must have been something that stirred up my hon. friends from the west to make the observations they did, particularly the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff). We in the maritime provinces believe that we have a good record behind us in respect to our feelings and actions towards the west. In 1870 they had some trouble in the west. I ask my hon. friends from the west: who were foremost in quelling the trouble that occurred in those days: Were not volunteer red coats from Nova Scotia to the fore in quelling that rebellion, and standing up manfully for the rights of the people of the west? In 1885 another trouble occurred in the northwest, and the same thing happened; the boys from Nova Scotia willingly and manfully volunteered to stand all the hardships that were necessary, to risk their lives within the zone of fire, defending the interests of the people of the west
and the rights of Canadians. That is the record of our feelings and conduct towards the west. I do not think that if my hon. friends would read the history of those days, they would likely speak about us as if we had no interest in the west. Our interests in the west have grown very materially since those days, the number of our people who have gone to the west has increased during the last 20 and 25 years, and for that reason our love for the west and our interest in the west have proportionately increased as the years have gone by. For that reason, I think this idea of sectionalism must be wiped out, and anything that has been said along that line must be understood as not having been said at all.
The Minister of Public Works, distinguished and able lawyer as he is, will understand that there are many -cases where the courts of law will find that a statute must be construed in a certain way, and that decisions will be given in such a manner as to take away rights and equities which were understood to be safeguarded by the principles and rules of the statute which is under interpretation. The learned Minister of Public Works no doubt knows that on several occasions, on scores of occasions, people have come back a second time to the legislature to get another enactment to take the place of one that had been legally construed by the courts, and so to change it that the original intention would be borne out by the subsequent legislation. That is very largely the position which is taken by the hon. mover of the resolution and the hon mover of the amendment which are before the House, because there is very little difference between them. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the principle adopted at con-feds ration was not the principle of absolute representation by population. The principle of representation by population was only adopted, as some other things were adopted at confederation, subject to stipulations. For instance, in the British North America Act the subject of education is absolutely given over to the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. If you stop there, you would think that this House has nothing to do with the question of education. But you will find that the subject is hemmed in by certain conditions which make it impossible for a local legislature to legislate on the question of education as they may see fit, they must have regard to the stipulations attached to that particular proposition in the British North America Act. Upon the same principle, it is stated here in the terms of confederation that representation shall be based upon population; but if that were so without any restriction at all, what is the sense of this

subsection 4 of section 51? It would have no meaning at all. We must suppose that it was put there for a purpose, and the purpose which I see was that of safeguarding the smaller provinces against the effect of representation by population. We find that absolute representation by population would take away some of the privileges we had at confederation, and this was put in to safeguard them. That subsection 4 of section 51 was to be interpreted of course as it was then understood, together with the section which defines what Canada was territorially; and we submit that properly defining that section 4 which says Canada shall be, or as considered to be, we would still retain our representation; that is our contention. We say: Give this Act the reasonable and equitable interpretation which was put upon iti by the fathers of confederation and we will not lose any members at all. Since then four has been converted into nine. Other conditions have come into consideration and the court of highest appeal in our country has said that this safeguard is not enough, it does not protect us at all when the aggregate is turned from the four provinces into nine. The aggregate is so great that five per cent or one-twentieth of the whole is not enough to safeguard our representation.
I say that purely in a court of equity and seeking equity as we come to this House, we have a right to say: If you have enlarged the aggregate from four to nine, you have a right to give us a safeguard in place of the insufficient old one that will protect for us and preserve for us the same ratio of representation which we had when we came into confederation. While that may be an absolutely bad argument in law, as: it probably is in view of the decision of the Privy Council, it is a proper argument in equity to lay before this House in asking for fair and equitable treatment, and beyond that we are not looking for anything.
I could understand the disappointment of a member for any province if what we are seeking would deprive them of a single representative in any part of Canada. I cannot understand that it does, I submit that it does not. The unit of representation remains the same, that is all they need be concerned about. In Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia, Alberta or any other province outside the maritime provinces, disappointment might be. caused if the unit of representation was to be disturbed. It is not to be disturbed and therefore they will get the same number of members whether we have less or more; it does not strike them in any way, their population will be divided by 65 as the Quebec representation is to remain fixed at 65. Therefore, the other provinces will get their number of members according as their, Mr. McKENZIE.
population bears a ratio to the population of Quebec and they need not be concerned about where we are, it does not take a single member from them. I could understand further that if the number of members who are to constitute this House was fixed they would have reason to find fault, they could say: There is only a place for 181 members, as the original agreement provided, and therefore if there are 15 or 18 from Nova Scotia, there will never be room for us, and it is only fair that they should be put out in order to make room for our representatives. That is not the condition, and therefore that argument falls to the ground because there is no limit upwards to the number of members who may compose this House. Yet it may well be said that this House should not be constituted of a smaller number of members than the number named at confederation. Therefore, as the unit remains the same, as we must make room for the members in this House as occasion requires-a larger House must be built if necessary-no man need be afraid that any group or unit of his people will remain unrepresented, because we have the same number of members we had at confederation, or because there is no room for them in this House. Therefore, unless it be on the question of allowance to members or some expense attached to a greater number of members, I cannot understand where it in the slightest degree touches the right of any province or increases or lessens the number of representatives outside of the provinces asking to be dealt with in this amendment. For that reason I cannot appreciate the objections taken on the grounds that have been set forth by the hon. members for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) and Saskatoon (Mr. Me- * Craney). I think it is fair to say that those fathers of confederation who came from the maritime provinces expected that they would have at least the same representation they had at that time. In my own province of Nova Scotia, we can readily understand why we had nineteen members. In those days we had a member from each county, and could not think of having less. The city and county of Halifax had two members. Therefore, our representatives from Nova Scotia agreed upon having the same number of members here that we had at that time. The political division of the province into counties had much to do with it. If we had had twelve counties I suppose we would only be looking for twelve members, and it was never intended that any of our counties should be deprived of their representation. When two counties are joined together in one constituency in Nova Scotia, it is looked upon as if one or both were to some extent disfranchised. If the old member for one county gets the united seat, the other part of the constitu-

ency feels itself more or less disfranchised. Take the county of Shelbourne, take the county of Victoria which I represent, and I think Pictou which formerly had two members. Victoria feels very keenly that it has been deprived of its member. If it can be done, without interfering with the rights of any other part of Canada, it would seem best for the sake of peace and harmony if that which was the intention of the fathers of confederation could be continued.
1 would say to my hon. friends who object to the proposal we make-why do they sit in the House for one day with the condition in the Act in respect to British Columbia. I have not heard any one finding fault in respect to that province, and yet that is all we are asking, simply that the condition in the Act in respect to British Columbia, shall be applied to us in the maritime provinces. The representation in British Columbia can never be reduced below the number of members with which it came into this union. My friends in the west are right in touch with the province of British Columbia. They do not regard that provision as unconstitutional or as militating against them, and if that condition of things in British Columbia cannot be regarded as unfair to the people of the west, how can similar conditions concerning what we regard as our rights in the maritime provinces be regarded as in any way infringing on any rights they may think themselves entitled to under the constitution. We do not want in the slightest way to cause any friction in this country, but I think it is our duty to our people to lay our case before this House, the highest and last tribunal to which we as Canadians can come, and to ask the powers that be, in their wisdom, to deal with it as in the best interests of the country.

FRASER (Kings, P.E.I.) Mr. Speaker, the history of this whole matter has been so well set before the House by hon. gentlemen from the maritime provinces who have already spoken that anything I might say would be repetition, and a3 I do not believe in reiterating arguments which have already been forcibly advanced, my remarks shall be brief. This question vitally affects the interests of the maritime provinces and more especially my own province of Prince Edward Island. The hon. gentleman, (Mr. Warburton) who moved this amendment, has been for a long period of years identified with the public life of our province, and every unprejudiced mind must give great weight to any declaration which he may make concerning our provincial affairs. Let any unprejudiced man in this parliament ask himself:	Would the fathers of confederation
have entered the union had they known that conditions wnich at present face us
would have arisen, and the answer must be, no.
