Read the correspondence, read the utterances of the public men of the period, read the newspaper comments, and in all these it appears most forcibly that were it known to the representatives of the maritime provinces at the confederation conference, that in time to come the representation of these provinces would be reduced, confederation would not have been accomplished. I am surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff) and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) with regard to this motion. I believe that the western members are blessed with a spirit of fair play, and I know that if they study the question they must conclude that no harm can arise to their provinces by conceding that which we justly demand. All we _ ask is that the original compact upon which we entered the union be carried out in its spirit. The hon. member for Assini-boia said that the representation of the province of Ontario had been reduced since confederation, but I think he is mistaken in that; and that only the maritime provinces are in this unfortunate position. We appeal to the sense of British fair plijy of hon. members of this House not to allow this injury to be done to the maritime provinces, and we ask them to aid us in getting redress. Let me tell the government that this question will not be settled until it is properly settled; let me tell the government that this question will not down; and that the longer relief is deferred the more troublesome it will become. It may be-I trust the day will never come-but it may be that some day this will become a burning question between the east and the west. We do not seek to injure the west; we helped to build up the west, and we spent our hard earned money in that endeavour. We of the east opened up the west and gave these people the great advantages they now enjoy, and would it be unnatural that they should now seek to penalize the provinces that brought them into existence. When the Hon. Mr. Pugsley wa3 in the New Brunswick government he took a very strong ground on this question, but I am sorry to see that to some extent he has receded from his then position. There are no two men in the House more conversant with this whole question than the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice; because when the former was Attorney General of New Brunswick he urged the cause of his province, and the Minister of Justice himself was retained by the legislature of Prince Edward Island to plead our cause before the Privy Council of England. The Privy Council unfortunately decided against us, and now we appeal to this parliament to give us the equity we-

are entitled to. The hon. the Minister of Public Works, in referring to this question, and mark you after the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council had decided against the contention of New Brunswick, used these words:
In the course of the argument before the Privy Council one of the law lords admitted that if Newfoundland should seek admission to the union she would have the right to stipulate as regards the terms and in respect to representation. How have our rights been taken away by the legislation of the Dominion. The only justification for it is that it was done by the authority of imperial orders in council or imperial statutes at the request of the government of Canada. When British Columbia was admitted into the union it was stipulated that her representation should be increased under the terms of the British North America Act, and that the Act should apply as if she had been one of the original provinces of the confederation. The same thing was done with respect to Manitoba. Now what has been the effect of this. It is that you must construe the British North America Act as if these provinces had been in the union in 1867. If that is so the compact of confederation has been violated by legislation and by orders in council without our being consulted. Surely the authorities at Ottawa should see that this wrong is remedied.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the authorities at Ottawa to-day is the Hon. Mr. Pugsiey, who then declared that Ottawa [DOT]should right this wrong, and, on this same subject the same hon. gentleman further said:
Therefore, when we raise the question of representation it is not that we are opposed to Quebec, but because we desire to preserve our rights and to maintain some degree of political influence in the east.
Again he said:
It does not seem to me that in view of the legislation which has already taken place, so seriously affecting our interests, and in view of what is now being done in connection with the legislation for the Northwest Territories, this government is yet doing its duty in asking the legislature to express its views and to endeavour to undo this great wrong.
These are the sentiments which were expressed in the year 1905 toy the Hon. Minister of Public Works in the legislative halls of his own province of New Brunswick. Now that he is one of the authorities at Ottawa, I would expect, and I think we should all expect, that he will continue to entertain these views. I will close by asking the members of this House, if they are not prepared to vote in favour of this resolution now, to study the question, and they will find that there is nothing in the resolution to do wrong or injury to any other province in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not know that my hon. friend wanted an immediate answer, and I have no objection to give my view of the case. I do not admit at all that when the boundaries between Ontario and Quebec and between Quebec and the rest of Canada were settled by statute in 1898, that was done with the view of increasing the territory of the province of Quebec. It was done to settle a dispute as to where the boundary was between Quebec and the rest of Canada.

I ayn not in a position to contradict the right hon. gentleman, nor would I do so, but according to the census returns of 1871, the area of the province of Quebec was shown to be some 193,000 square miles, and the area of Quebec today is stated as 351,000 square miles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All this is conjecture. It never was asserted.

According also to the recognized maps of the period just following confederation, we find that the province of Quebec was very differently outlined from what it is at present. Further, let me read from 'Hansard' of March 30, 1905, a speech delivered by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) in which he says, with reference to this very matter:
If there is any doubt as to the statement I have made, I would like to lay before the House a few extracts from an order in council of the Quebec government, dated the 24th April, 1898, upon which the legislation was subsequently framed. Attached to this order in council is a report from Mr. E. H. Taclie, assistant commissioner of Crown lands, who, after discussing the question as to the province of Quebec making a demand for that portion of the coast of Labrador which is under the jurisdiction of Newfoundland, goes on to say:	The claiming of that territory

27:4
would result in serious diplomatic complications which the Dominion government certainly will not raise, but it seems to me that a compromise might be arrived at which will prove acceptable to all those interested. The claims under the old French regime, thus altered, would still include a vast extent of territory, which in extent and value wou'd be a good equivalent to the territory claimrd by Ontario. The claim might be framed in the following manner:
Mr. Tache then went on to define in detail the boundary line as it was finally adopted in the Bill passed by this parliament, and he said:
The definition of the limits means an increase in area of 116,550 square miles. In my opinion to go further, as far as the Hudson straits would be too grasping.
That is what I base my opinion upon. In 1908, a resolution was adopted by this House to add to the province of Quebec a portion at least of the territory known as Ungava, and at the same time to add to Ontario and Manitoba the southern portion of the very vast district of Keewatin. I only mention this to show that the province of Quebec has had its territory considerably enlarged, and that, should that additional territory become populated, the unit of representation will be changed and changed very prejudicially to the maritime provinces. Although to-day the land is barren and seemingly inhospitable, no man can say that in its icy grasp there may not be valuable minerals. Indeed we have fair authority for believing that there are, in all likelihood, gold and silver deposits, and even iron and coal there. One American professor, an enthusiast it may be, has gone so far as to say it probably contains diamonds. Well, we know what the discovery of any of these would mean. That discovery would be followed by development, and development means an increased population, so that there is nothing very improbable in the prospect of the addition of this territory considerably changing the unit of representation. To-day we are speaking hopefully of the construction of a railway to Hudson bay, of which no one 25 or 30 years ago would have dreamt the possibility. There is therefore no argument in saying that this territory is not likely to have a large population at any time, or may not figure in the representation to the extent of altering the unit. In this connectiort let me say that the maritime provinces have also some claim to this vast territory purchased from the Hudson Bay Company in 1869, for the sum of $1,500,000 and that in any further disposition of that territory the rights of the maritime provinces, as partners to the extent of their original partnership interest, should be recognized. The maritime provinces are sea-girt, so that their natural boundaries are fixed and determined and they cannot expand their i
Mr, JAMESON.
population by any extension of their boundaries. Therefore they are not likely to grow so fast as the other provinces. My hon. friend from Kings' (Mr. Fraser) has referred to the building up of the west at the expense of the east. No doubt if there had been no east, we would have no west. We know that opening up of the territories, the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, and the vast inflow of immigration were things not fully contemplated when confederation was formed, and not consider, ed in their great effect when the British North America Act was framed. But despite that fact a saving clause was put into the British North America Act, and it was only by the Act of 1886 that that saving clause was taken away, or its effect destroyed.
The fact that British Columbia was given a minimum of representation seems to me fair ground why we should ask for similar treatment for the maritime provinces. The argument that in order to do so we should change the unit of representation from Quebec to the maritime provinces does not seem to me well taken, and that is the only argument which can be put forward against the conceding of the very reasonable proposition advanced by the hon. gentleman who has moved the amendment to the resolution. It seems to me that for another reason too, the maritime provinces are entitled to fair and reasonable consideration from this parliament, At a time when the political fabric of old Canada was tottering to its very foundations, when the statesmen of the day were unable to find a common ground on which to uprear a lasting government, in fact when the very fate of the country seemed to be trembling in the balance, they looked to the Atlantic coast, there they saw the Atlantic provinces, their people happy, prosperous and progressive, their statesmen, wise, firm and far-sighted. The maritime provinces were called in to redress the balance of the old Canadas. Confederation became an accomplished fact, a firm and stable government was erected. The maritime provinces may be said to have saved the situation. That larger Canada gave to the statesmen of the day the courage and to this Dominion the resources and standing in the money markets of England to enter upon the great national undertakings which were then begun and are still going forward with giant strides. I do not think, Bir, that the people of old Canada or of the new west will deny to the maritime provinces who undoubtedly made sacrifices to render these things possible; that mead of recognition in this House which the founders of confederation evidently considered they should have. And I trust that the amendment to this resolution, for the various reasons advanced to-day, will carry, and that the matter will not be deferred as has been intimated.

1 think there is little doubt that most people of generous disposition will regard this question as one of equity rather than of law. While it may fairly be admitted that there are elements which have been brought into the situation since the original compact was entered into by the four provinces that disturb the relations of to-day and make them different from what they would have been had the original compact been adhered to closely, still I do not think there is anything in it that seems to give them a legal right-if a layman may be permitted to express an opinion on a question of law. to entitle them to the consideration asked for. But thinking it over it seems to me that the four original provinces might well claim that in our representation here we will adhere to the right which we secured at confederation of having our representation struck by the census of these four provinces, excluding all other provinces, and according to the unit of representation ascertained by dividing the population of Quebec on a basis of 65. Ascertain the unit of representation and by that means determine the number of members each of the maritime provinces should have. But I do not think that Prince Edward Island can claim the same right, because that province came in afterward, and the Act provides that any province which might come in afterwards would come in upon the terms of the agreement that was come to by its own legislature and the federal authority. Prince Edward Island came to some understanding, and that understanding was embodied in the agreement. That is, Prince Edward Island made its terms according to the judgments of its legislature and came in under that Act passed in accordance with those terms. And one of these terms was the unit of representation. It has been cited here tonight that when Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia came in it destroyed the proportion. Well I think that is a fair and reasonable contention. I listened to the figures given by the hon. member for York, N.B., (Mr. Crocket) when he said that if representation had been given at the last decennial census, ascertained on the basis of the population of the four original provinces of confederation, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would be quite satisfied. I think they have a right to claim that, regardless of what principle was adopted in giving the other provinces representation, and that it is not in justice to the other provinces if that right is conceded to them, for it is in their bond and they have a right to look for the fulfilment of the conditions of their bond. There is another thing, that has disturbed the relative strength of these provinces in this House. We provided for Manitoba, and Saskatchewan and Alberta taking a census every five years and having their representation rearranged according to the increase of population. The British North America Act provides for redistribution every ten years. Here is another element in this situation that disturbs the balance to the disadvantage of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
In view of these considerations, it seemed to me it would not be unreasonable or very much out of place if this parliament should take it up and give to these smaller provinces a proportionately larger representation than the larger provinces have. That is a principle that obtains in all deliberate assemblies. In our county councils in Ontario we provide that any township with a population of one thousand shall send one reeve to the county council; if it has more it sends a deputy reeve, if still more two deputy reeves; but the smaller townships are given a larger representation proportionately than the larger one. In the United States they follow the same principle in regard to the smaller states of the union, and in legislative representation, and in even the election of the President. they are given a larger proportionate share of power than the more populous states. That seems to be in harmony with the idea that the weaker shall have something to help them in addition to their own strength. I do not feel that the maritime provinces are depending only upon the number of their representatives or that the influence they exercise in the House is simply through the men who are sent here by the votes of the people of those provinces. For, as an hon. member has pointed out, many maritime province people have gone to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and helped to develop that country, some of them have done so well that the electors of their several districts have sent them back here as representatives for those districts. I have no doubt that when they come here and take part in the deliberations of this House they will not forget the fact that they are natives of Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick, or Prince Edward Island and will exercise, it may be a silent, but nevertheless a potent influence on behalf of their native provinces in addition to the influence which they exercise as representatives of their constituencies in the west. So they have a little additional influence in this House beyond what mere numbers would seem to indicate. So with regard to the influence we have in the Senate. Come to the province of Ontario. Quebec wisely provided that her province should be divided up into various districts with a senator for each one. But we did not make the same provision in Ontario; therefore, in the rural districts, there are large areas which are unrepresented by a senator, and when you

speak of representing a given district, we have no representation in the Senate from any of those districts. But as the larger number of the representatives in the Senate reside in the cities, they are still representatives of the province, they have their interests in the various portions of the province and in making a calculation how many shall be in this House from the cities we do not give the same proportionate representation as the country districts Why? Because a large number of senators and members reside in the cities, they have the larger share of their property in the cities, and they look after the interests of the cities as well as of the rural districts. We have no rural districts represented in Ontario, in the same sense rural districst are represented in the province of Quebec. The same remark applies to the maritime provinces, some of whose population has wandered off to the northwest, and are coming back here as representatives from those various districts. I think there is some thing in the enlargement of the province of Quebec as one of the disturbing elements, it is a factor at least that may be regarded as an element of the situation. The first minister said that it was only in 1878 that we determined what was the boundary line. Well, we passed an Act declaring it, but it was never determined, as it ought to be, by some tribunal established for that purpose. We determined the boundary line between Canada and the United States, not by an arbitration, but by men selected to ascertain where the boundary was. I have no remembrance that we ever appointed' any commission of experts to determine exactly where the boundary was between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; but we determined it by Act of parliament, and by so doing we enlarged very much the province of Quebec. It was admitted in this House that we were enlarging the province of Quebec, and when a desire was afterwards expressed to have the province of Manitoba extended it was said that we had enlarged the province of Quebec, but we refused to enlarge the province of Manitoba. We did not determine by any tribunal exactly where the boundary line was between the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec, but we made practically an arbitrary boundary by federal statute. In speaking now, I am saying very little with reference to the resolution except as regards the equity of the claim. It always did seem to me that there was some equity in the claim; and speaking personally, and judging by public sentiment, I do not think the larger provinces would be averse to conceding to the smaller provinces the right never to have their representation less than it was when they entered confederation.
Mr. SPROULE

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I believe this day has been very profitably spent in discussing a question which is growing in importance to a certain portion of the Dominion. This is above all things a maritime question, it affects the maritime provinces. The resolution is intended to deal exclusively with the maritime provinces. It reads thus:
That in the opinion of this House the maritime provinces of Canada should have preserved to them the representation in the House of Commons that they now enjoy. That in the redistribution of constituencies to be made after the next decennial census the number of representatives to be returned from the said provinces should not in any case be reduced.	.
This motion has been prompted by the fact that as a consequence of the two last censuses the representation of the maritime provinces has been decreased on each occasion. Prince Edward Island has lost one man, Nova Scotia has lost four or five, and New Brunswick three or four. If that motion had been adhered to, I think it would have been more favourably received than it can be with the amendment added. The amendment which is to take the place of the original motion, reads thus:
Each province of the Dominion of Canada shall have as a minimum representation in the House of Commons the representation it had upon becoming a province of Canada, and in the redistribution of constituencies to be made after the next, and after every decennial census, the representation of each province shall not be any less than that minimum.
I never heard any expression of opinion asking for a change in our present constitution except from the maritime provinces. I do not see any reason why there should be such a change applied to Ontario, or to any other province. I can see some reason why such a change should be made with regard to the maritime provinces. Therefore, so far as my judgment goes, the only way in which it can be approached is on the lines laid down by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, and repeated by the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule), that is to say, that the maritime provinces, in view of the peculiar position which they occupy, ought to command a generous treatment from the other provinces. Now, I would like the House to remember that confederation was a compact originally, and must remain a compact between province and province. When the first four started the work of confederation together they agreed' upon certain conditions. I have listened carefully to this debate, with the exception of a, little time when I was called out; I have listened to the arguments which have been brought forward by hon. gentlemen who have spoken to the resolution. They have

not all been conducive to the resolution, and some of the arguments in support of the amendment have been conducive to the motion. I must say that I differ altogether from the arguments of my hon. friends from the maritime provinces when they assert that they are labouring under an injustice. I cannot see where the injustice lies. They say the injustice lies in the fact that when they entered confederation it was stipulated that the unit of representation should be the representation of the province of Quebec, which was then apportioned between four provinces, and that the unit of representation has been changed by the fact that it is now apportioned between nine provinces instead of four. Now, if there is one thing more certain than another, it is that historically there is not a shadow of doubt that when the four provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, made the original compact of confederation, they had no idea that the Dominion would always be composed of those four provinces only, they certainly contemplated that other provinces would join them. Section 146 makes this as plain as it can be:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, on addresses from the Houses of the parliament of Canada, and from the Houses of the respective legislatures of the colonies or provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia to admit those colonies or provinces, or any of them, into the union.
Therefore when the four provinces made the original contract it was contemplated that Prince Edward Island should come in, that Newfoundland should come in, that British Columbia should come in. When each one of these provinces was to come in under, what terms and conditions was it to come in? It was to come in under certain terms and conditions to be agreed upon by themselves but always subject to the original contract. These are the very words:
On such terms and conditions in each case as are in the addresses expressed and as the Queen thinks fit to approve, subject to the provisions of this Act.
What was one of the provisions of this Act? One of these provisions, and it was an important one, was in regard to this veTy item of representation. How was it to be done? Every time that a new member was joined to confederation, an apportionment was to be made on the unit determined by Quebec, but to be apportioned between four, five, six, seven, eight or nine provinces as the case might be. Provision was made for the admission of the three provinces then in existence, and provision was made also for the acquisition of Rupert's land and the Hudson Bay country, and with what object? With the object,
accomplished since, of making provinces, and it also has been determined legally by the Privy Council and historically that what had applied to confederation was to extend to the provinces, that every new province coming in was to have the same rights, privileges and restrictions as the other provinces.
The difficulty, however, has arisen from this point, that the provinces by the sea have not developed as rapidly as the other provinces. You would not hear of this motion being made to-day if the provinces by the sea had developed as rapidly and had been able to keep their representation. But Quebec moved more rapidly, Ontario and the other provinces in the western part of the country all moved more rapidly, and the consequence was that as every other province had its representation increased, the representation of the maritime provinces was decreased. They ask for some remedy. They cannot have it in law, they cannot have it, so far as I can see, in the arguments which they have advanced. The only way in which they can have a remedy is, as I said a moment ago, to apply to the other provinces, more potent than they are, with larger representation, to give them some equivalent to what has been given to British Columbia. The members from the maritime provinces must remember that representation by population was a bone of contention in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec for something like 20 years. It did not bring on a revolution, but it almost brought on a revolution, and at last it was conceded that no fairer and no more equitable principle with regard to representation could be found than population. What principle can be fairer than every province which is represented on the floor of this parliament should be represented according to the number of its population? It is impossible to find or to imagine a principle more equitable than this one. And you propose now to limit it. In what way? In regard to the other provinces. I very much doubt if the other provinces would agree to limit it in any way, and moreover, I say to my hon. friends from the maritime provinces, that the principle is fair and equitable and cannot be gainsaid on that ground. But it is another story if you say to me: The provinces by the sea are small compared with the others, they have not the same opportunity of expansion as the others have, they cannot extend their territory, they are necessarily limited; the territory of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, and the other provinces, can be increased because there is a large territory behind them, but the provinces by the sea are cramped, and therefore they cannot increase, and it can be claimed in equity or fairness that it is not a matter of concern to the other provinces, if their representation is kept up to the

limit as at the time of confederation, because the other provinces have become so large that even if the maritime provinces are granted that small privilege the balance between, province and province would not be seriously affected and the preponderance of one province over the other would not suffer. This is a view with which, for my part, I would be disposed to agree, but 1 have to say also that there is great force in the contention of my friend, a force absolute, a force paramount in my judgment, that it would not be in the right spirit of the Confederation Act that the parliament of Canada should undertake to disturb in any way the principle laid down in the British North America Act as to the representation of every province in this parliament unless the other provinces have been consulted. I do not think, for instance, that an amendment of this kind should be taken up by this parliament unless all the other provinces had had an opportunity to express their opinion on it, and for this reason I think it is well that we should pause and look about before we go further into this.
I may repeat that I welcome this discussion. I am sorry that the time has come now that we must adjourn, because I would like to hear more about it. I am sorry that we have not heard from the other provinces. We have not heard from Ontario or Quebec, we have heard from only two of the provinces, other than the maritime provinces, and, therefore, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.

I understand that the Minister of Railways is to make his statement to-morrow?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER Yes, the Minister of Railways and Canals, in view of the fact that Mr. Butler, the deputy minister, has taken another position, would like to dispose of the estimates. He will premise that with the usual statement in regard to the railway. The discussion on that may possibly take more than one day.
I had intended to take up the Naval Bill on Wednesday, but in case this other debate is not concluded to-morrow, I propose to take it on Thursday next.

It does not appear that there is any provision for a report by the present board of management of the Intercolonial railway. That is due, I presume, to the fact that the board has been constituted under the general powers of management conferred upon the Minister of Railways and Canals by the Act respect- [DOT] Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
ing the Intercolonial railway. It would be desirable, it seems to me, that such a report should always be presented to parliament. That is merely a matter of administrative order by the minister, assuming he has the power under the statute to which I have referred. No such report has been laid before us up to the present time, and I trust that the minister, when he makes his statement, will at least give us every item of information which might reasonably be expected if those commissioners were bound under the terms of the statute to make a formal written report to parliament
